messages.subject: Issue on mixedmirt: second-order test
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I'm fitting a model using 'mixedmirt' with 5 factors, several fixed effects and random intercepts, the latter are different for each factor (through arguments 'lr.fixed' and 'lr.random').

The estimation algorithm always converges, but I get the following message:

"Second-order test: model is not a maximum or the information matrix is too inaccurate"

I see I get very low average acceptance rates (some are very close to 0). Do you retain it could be a problem of 'not mixing too well', then potentially fixed by working on 'MHcand'?

Many thanks in advance.
Simone

messages.subject: M2 with missing data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,
Thank you very much for implementing M2 statistics for missing data in the 1.42 version. It was one of the best improvements in mirt for years!
However, I am concerned about how M2 is estimated as I am unaware of publishing the index for such a purpose. Is it documented elsewhere?

I have this question: In a performance test parameterized using the GPCM/PCM model (composed of super-items scored 0-5), there is an ending rule (administration stops after five minutes). Therefore, the participants with the highest performance reached all the items, while they also usually had the highest score on all the items. Thus, the probability of missing correlates with the measured ability. I am aware of problems with MAR and know my estimates could be biased, and this is not the question.

If I estimate M2* statistics in the Rasch model, it looks as expected with a good fit. However, if I estimate C2 statistics, it's odd; C2 statistics are too high to be real (like x2/df = 20000, RMSEA > 1.3, and TLI/CFI values are excellent.
I know why C2 and M2* differ (considering the univariate-collapsed frequencies), but such a difference is strange. I cannot check it in the 2PL model directly due to the small number of df, but if I collapse the lowest (rarely used) categories, I get a similar pattern.

So, my question is, how exactly is C2/M2* estimated with missing data?

Under this parameterisation the intercepts are more reflective of category endorsement frequencies/probabilities, so the larger negative values have more to do with the observations that few individuals selected those categories. I wouldn't consider this a problem at all, and I imagine if you used something like mirt::itemstats(dat) you'll see very few responses in those large negative intercept categories.

If it helps, you can play around with the nominal model parameters interactively via mirt::itemplot(shiny=TRUE), which might help you see the meaning of the intercepts when modified. Cheers.

Phil

P.S. If you're interested in reporting standardized information from the NRM I'd recommend installing the dev version as I recently patched this behaviour to be more consistent.

messages.subject: Re: M2 with missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hynek,

This was indeed a bug in the code for C2, which did not correctly track the proportion of missing information in some of the computations, particularly the first-order table of counts. I've pushed the fix to the dev version and made a note in the NEWS file. See the simulation at the end for the corrected behaviour.

There's nothing really fancy about how mirt estimates M2/C2 with missing data. The generalization was that rather than using functions like cov() and mean() to compute proportion information the cross-product and counts were used directly so that they are allowed to be unequal. It's difficult to go through things in text, but the the idea is that the observed moments should be allowed to vary as a function of the marginal/bivariate tables of counts, while the on the model expectations side things are generally computed normally but rescaled where necessary as proportion of the missing data. There are, however, some more dodgy outputs like the reporting of RMSEA, which I'm not exactly sure how to properly modify with missing data as the formula typically works with a single N.... HTH for now.

Phil

```r
devtools::install_github('philchalmers/mirt')

# requires version 1.43.4+
library(mirt)

a <- matrix(rlnorm(20,.2,.3))

# for the graded model, ensure that there is enough space between the intercepts,
# otherwise closer categories will not be selected often (minimum distance of 0.3 here)
diffs <- t(apply(matrix(runif(20*4, .3, 1), 20), 1, cumsum))
diffs <- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
d <- diffs + rnorm(20)

dat <- simdata(a, d, 5000, itemtype = 'graded')

mod.full <- mirt(dat)

# 50% missing at random
cases <- prod(dim(dat))
dat.miss <- dat
dat.miss[sample(1:cases, cases * .50)] <- NA
head(dat.miss)

mod.miss <- mirt(dat.miss)

# these should be very close
M2(mod.full)
M2(mod.miss)

M2(mod.full, type = 'C2')
M2(mod.miss, type = 'C2')
```

messages.subject_clean: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

Your approach sounds reasonable to me. However, I do wonder how you went about managing the time factor in this design as technically each time point reflects some type of potential change in the individuals (even the in the control group, whose traits may be influenced by regression to the mean effects). I would think of this design as one where you have three highly correlated traits due to the three measurement occasions, where by construction the items are treated invariant over time (at least initially) while the traits are allowed to have different means/variances per group. Once the scaling effects over time are taken into account in the model then you can move into the DIF testing flavour by removing one or more item parameter constraints over the measurement occasions.

Of course, you can focus on one point at a time as well, which would also get at the idea of measurement invariance within each occasion, though I would worry about family-wise error control as that's a lot of testing .... HTH for now.

# Define the model: Three latent traits (one for each time point: Pretest, Posttest, Follow-Up)
model <- '
  Trait1 = 1-11  # Pretest
  Trait2 = 1-11  # Posttest
  Trait3 = 1-11  # Follow-Up
  COV = Trait1*Trait2*Trait3  # Allow correlations between traits
'

# Step 1: Fit the initial model assuming measurement invariance
# (All items are treated as invariant across groups and time points)
model_invariant <- multipleGroup(
  data,                # Dataset containing item responses
  model,               # Model structure with three latent traits
  group = Grpvect,     # Grouping variable (e.g., intervention vs. control group)
  itemtype = 'graded', # Graded response model for polytomous items
  invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts")  # Fix slopes and intercepts across groups
)
summary(model_invariant)

# Step 2: Check scaling effects
# Extract group-specific means and variances for the three latent traits
scaling_effects <- coef(model_invariant, simplify = TRUE)$GroupPars
print(scaling_effects)
# Interpretation: Differences in means (MEAN_1, MEAN_2, MEAN_3) or variances (VAR_1, VAR_2, VAR_3)
# indicate potential group or time-point effects.

# Step 3: Relax the invariance for specific items flagged for DIF
# (Based on prior DIF analysis, allow parameters for W_5C, W_6A, and W_9A to vary)
model_DIF <- multipleGroup(
  data,                # Dataset containing item responses
  model,               # Model structure with three latent traits
  group = Grpvect,     # Grouping variable
  itemtype = 'graded', # Graded response model for polytomous items
  invariance = c(
    "slopes", "intercepts",     # General invariance for most items
    "W_5C", "W_6A", "W_9A"      # Allow these items to vary across groups (DIF testing)
  )
)
summary(model_DIF)

# Step 4: Conduct DIF and DTF analyses
# Evaluate item-level DIF and overall test-level bias
DRF_results <- DRF(
  model_DIF,         # Updated model with relaxed invariance
  draws = 1000,      # Number of Monte Carlo draws for confidence intervals
  DIF = TRUE,        # Include DIF testing
  p.adjust = "BH"    # Adjust p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method
)

> Hi Hynek,
>
> This was indeed a bug in the code for C2, which did not correctly track the proportion of missing information in some of the computations, particularly the first-order table of counts. I've pushed the fix to the dev version and made a note in the NEWS file. See the simulation at the end for the corrected behaviour.
>
> There's nothing really fancy about how mirt estimates M2/C2 with missing data. The generalization was that rather than using functions like cov() and mean() to compute proportion information the cross-product and counts were used directly so that they are allowed to be unequal. It's difficult to go through things in text, but the the idea is that the observed moments should be allowed to vary as a function of the marginal/bivariate tables of counts, while the on the model expectations side things are generally computed normally but rescaled where necessary as proportion of the missing data. There are, however, some more dodgy outputs like the reporting of RMSEA, which I'm not exactly sure how to properly modify with missing data as the formula typically works with a single N.... HTH for now.
>
> Phil
>
>
> ```r
> devtools::install_github('philchalmers/mirt')
>
> # requires version 1.43.4+
> library(mirt)
>

> # otherwise closer categories will not be selected often (minimum distance of 0.3 here)

> diffs <- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
> d <- diffs + rnorm(20)
>
> dat <- simdata(a, d, 5000, itemtype = 'graded')
>
> mod.full <- mirt(dat)
>
>
> # 50% missing at random
> cases <- prod(dim(dat))
> dat.miss <- dat
> dat.miss[sample(1:cases, cases * .50)] <- NA
> head(dat.miss)
>
> mod.miss <- mirt(dat.miss)
>
> # these should be very close
> M2(mod.full)
> M2(mod.miss)
>
> M2(mod.full, type = 'C2')

> ```
